newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG general storms out of mercenary inquiry.
newsitem.headline: PNG general storms out of mercenary inquiry.

text.p: The Papua New Guinea general who led an army rebellion against a government plan to use mercenaries on Bougainville island stormed out of a public inquiry on Wednesday after being called a liar.

Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, sacked as army chief over the rebellion, was told by government counsel at an inquiry into the mercenary fiasco that he had lied to PNG special forces troops over their future.
"I am not a liar, I am an officer and gentleman," Singirok told reporters after walking out of the hearing.
"I'm going home to Murray Barracks and I will not return until he apologises."

Singirok was at the centre of a 10-day political crisis in the South Pacific nation in March during which prime minister Sir Julius Chan, his deputy Chris Haiveta and Defence Minister Mathias Ijape were forced to stand aside.

In five days of testimony from Singirok, government counsel Marshall Cooke has been trying to cast doubt on Singirok's motives and to portray him as an inept commander whose failures on Bougainville forced Chan to arrange the US$36 million mercenary contract with Britain's Sandline International.
On Wednesday, Cooke cross-examined Singirok over an address he gave to special forces a week before he demanded Chan's resignation over the Sandline contract.
The inquiry heard earlier that the forces were told they were to form a special guard to protect Chan and other politicians.
But Singirok reacted angrily and shouted "don't call me a liar" when Cooke said he had lied to the unit over their future assignment.
The inquiry had been scheduled to end on Friday, but Chan and the other ministers have yet to testify and hearings are expected to carry on next week as well.
If the inquiry finds Chan did not bend government rules in awarding the secret contract, Chan could, in theory, return as prime minister before national elections due in June.
